title: Natural Language Processing
overview: Language is the hardest problem in AI. Making computers understand and generate human text requires solving meaning, context, ambiguity, and relationships between words — all at once. Learn how modern NLP went from counting words to the Transformer architecture that powers ChatGPT.

data.alt: Natural Language Processing Tasks overview showing NLP hub with connected task nodes

data.body: Natural Language Processing (NLP) is the field of AI that deals with understanding, interpreting, and generating human language.
NLP powers some of the most widely used AI systems: automatic summarization, machine translation, named entity recognition, speech recognition, text classification, and more.
But language is deceptively hard for computers. Ambiguity, context, idioms, sarcasm, and grammatical variation make it one of the deepest challenges in AI.

Natural Language Processing is the intersection of computer science, linguistics, and artificial intelligence. Its goal: enable computers to understand, interpret, and generate human language in a way that is both meaningful and useful.

Automatic summarisation, information extraction, language identification, machine translation, named entity recognition, speech recognition, text classification, and word sense disambiguation. Each task addresses a different dimension of language understanding.

Ambiguity: 'I saw the man with the telescope' has two meanings. Context: 'bank' means different things in 'river bank' vs 'bank account'. Sarcasm, idioms, and cultural references add even more layers of complexity.

From raw text to understanding: tokenisation splits text into units, parsing builds structure, semantic analysis extracts meaning, and pragmatic analysis considers context. Each stage adds a layer of understanding.

data.text: Language is the hardest problem in AI because it requires bridging the gap between the discrete, structured world of symbols and the continuous, messy world of meaning.

data.body: Syntax is the set of rules that govern the structure of sentences. It answers: 'Is this sentence grammatically well-formed?' Semantics is the study of meaning. It answers: 'What does this sentence actually mean?' These two dimensions are surprisingly independent — a sentence can be grammatically perfect but semantically nonsense, or semantically clear but grammatically broken.

data.text: The linguist Noam Chomsky famously illustrated this with the sentence: 'Colorless green ideas sleep furiously.' The sentence is grammatically perfect — it follows English syntax rules — but it is semantically meaningless. This proves that syntax and semantics are distinct systems in the brain.

data.body: Without syntax, an NLP model only sees a bag of words — losing subject-object relationships, modification, and sentence hierarchy. Consider: 'The dog bit the man' vs 'The man bit the dog.' The same words, the same bag-of-words representation — but completely different meanings. Syntax tells us who did what to whom.

data.text: The classic ambiguity example: 'I saw the man with the telescope'. Does the speaker have the telescope, or does the man? Syntax provides two different parse trees for the same string of words. Resolving this ambiguity requires understanding the semantic context.

blocks.title: Syntax Is the Framework, Semantics Fills the Rooms
blocks.subtitle: Watch how a building goes from steel beams to a living workspace — and see how syntax and semantics work the same way in language.

panels.label: Syntax Creates the Structure
panels.description: Syntax builds the framework that holds everything together. A building under construction has steel beams, pillars, and floors — it clearly has a shape, but it is not yet usable. There are no walls, no furniture, no people. The skeleton of the sentence takes shape: nouns, verbs, phrases — all locked into grammatical order.

panels.label: Same Structure, Still Empty
panels.description: A structure without meaning is complete in form but empty in purpose. The same building now has walls and rooms, but they are completely empty. No desks, no lights, no furniture, no activity. The structure exists, but there is no purpose. A sentence can be perfectly grammatical yet carry no real meaning — just as Chomsky's colorless green ideas sleep furiously has perfect syntax but zero sense.

panels.label: Semantics Gives Meaning
panels.description: Semantics gives the structure purpose, meaning, and real-world use. The exact same building is now fully furnished and alive. Offices are occupied, lights are on, people are working, meeting rooms buzz with conversation, and signs identify each room's purpose. The structure hasn't changed — only its meaning and function have. Semantics fills the grammatical framework with real-world significance.

blocks.insight: Syntax = the blueprint and framework (how something is organized). Semantics = what the organized structure actually means and is used for. The three-screen progression makes the distinction intuitive without relying on technical definitions.
blocks.reinforcement: Syntax builds the skeleton. Semantics brings it to life. A sentence needs both to communicate.

blocks.title: Why This Matters
blocks.body: Syntax and semantics are independent dimensions. A sentence can be grammatical but meaningless (like Chomsky's example), or meaningful but ungrammatical (like 'Me hungry'). NLP systems need to handle both dimensions to truly understand language.
bullets: Syntactic errors: grammar rules are broken
Semantic errors: meaning doesn't make sense
Real NLP must handle both types of errors simultaneously

data.body: A context-free grammar (CFG) is a formal system for describing the syntax of a language. It consists of a set of production rules that define how sentences can be built from smaller parts. Each rule has a single non-terminal symbol on the left and a sequence of terminals and non-terminals on the right.
A simple English CFG might look like this:

data.code:
S  → NP VP
NP → D N
VP → V NP
D  → "the" | "a"
N  → "cat" | "dog" | "city"
V  → "saw" | "chased" | "ate"
data.output: Grammar is defined by production rules. Each non-terminal (S, NP, VP, etc.) expands into terminals (words) or other non-terminals.

blocks.title: How Parsing Works
blocks.body: Given a CFG and a sentence, parsing is the process of finding a derivation — a sequence of rule applications — that produces the sentence. The result is a parse tree that shows the hierarchical structure of the sentence. The root of the tree is S (sentence), and the leaves are the actual words.
bullets: Each internal node is a non-terminal (S, NP, VP)
Each leaf node is a terminal word
The tree structure captures grammatical relationships
Ambiguous sentences have multiple possible parse trees

data.code:
S
      /   \
    NP     VP
   / \    / \
  D   N  V   NP
  |   |  |  / \
 the cat saw D  N
             |  |
            a  dog

Parse tree for 'the cat saw a dog'
Grammar rules used:
S  → NP VP
NP → D N
VP → V NP
D  → "the" | "a"
N  → "cat" | "dog"
V  → "saw" | "chased"
data.output: The parse tree shows step-by-step how the sentence follows the grammar. Each branching point is a rule application.

blocks.title: Grammar Rules Are Like Lego Building Instructions
blocks.subtitle: Lego instructions tell you how smaller pieces combine to form larger structures. Grammar rules do the same for words — combine nouns and verbs into phrases, and phrases into sentences.

panels.label: Words as Bricks
panels.description: A clean table with scattered LEGO pieces of different colors. Each piece has a word label: Dog (Noun), Runs (Verb), The (Article), Fast (Adjective), Park (Noun). Nothing is connected yet. Words are like individual LEGO pieces — each has a purpose, but alone they don't build much.

panels.label: Rules Connect Words
panels.description: A LEGO instruction booklet is open. Step 1: 'The' + 'Dog' snap together into Noun Phrase. Step 2: 'Runs' + 'Fast' snap together into Verb Phrase. Grammar rules act like LEGO instructions, showing which words can connect to form meaningful phrases.

panels.label: Phrases Become Sentence
panels.description: The assembled LEGO phrase blocks connect into a complete LEGO house. The roof is 'The Dog' (Noun Phrase). The walls are 'Runs Fast' (Verb Phrase). Everything clicks together: 'The Dog Runs Fast.' Grammar combines phrases into complete sentences, just as LEGO instructions combine pieces into a finished model.

blocks.insight: A finite set of grammar rules can generate an infinite number of sentences — just as a finite set of Lego pieces can build an infinite variety of models.
blocks.reinforcement: Grammar isn't about memorizing rules — it's the set of instructions that tells you how to assemble words into meaningful sentences.

data.body: Before any model can understand language, raw text must be converted into numbers. How you represent text determines what patterns a model can learn. The history of NLP is largely the history of improving text representations.

Text is split into tokens — words, subwords, or characters. Tokenisation is the first step. Modern models like GPT use subword tokenisation: common words are single tokens; rare words are split into meaningful chunks.

The simplest representation: count how many times each word appears and ignore word order entirely. 'The cat sat' and 'sat the cat' have identical representations. Useful for topic classification despite losing all syntactic information.

Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency: weight words by how often they appear in a document (TF) divided by how common they are across all documents (IDF). Words that are distinctive to a document get higher scores than words that appear everywhere.

The vocabulary is the complete set of unique tokens the model knows. Modern LLMs like GPT-4 have vocabularies of roughly 100,000 tokens. Any word not in the vocabulary must be broken down into subword tokens.

Text preprocessing cleans raw text before the model processes it. Garbage in, garbage out — clean input is essential. Lowercasing: convert all text to lowercase so 'The' and 'the' are treated the same. Reduces vocabulary size and improves consistency. Removing punctuation: strip periods, commas, and quotation marks — they add noise and rarely carry signal for most NLP tasks. Removing stop words: filter out common words like 'the', 'is', 'and' that appear in every document. They add little meaning but inflate representations. Tokenization: split text into smaller units (words, subwords, or characters) that the model can process individually. Stemming: chop off word endings to get the root form. 'Running', 'runner', and 'ran' all become 'run'. Fast but can produce non-real words. Lemmatization: reduce words to their dictionary base form using vocabulary analysis. 'Better' becomes 'good'. Slower than stemming but produces real words.

items: Stop Words — Common words (the, is, and) that are filtered out because they carry little semantic meaning.
Stemming — A fast, heuristic approach that chops word prefixes/suffixes to get the root form.
Lemmatization — A slower, vocabulary-aware approach that returns the dictionary base form of a word.

data.body: A token is the smallest unit of text that a model processes. Tokens can be words, subwords, or even individual characters. Word tokenization splits text on spaces and punctuation. Simple and intuitive, but fails on unknown words and treats 'run' and 'running' as different tokens. Sentence tokenization splits a document into individual sentences. Useful for tasks where sentence boundaries matter, like summarisation. Subword tokenization (used by GPT, BERT) splits rare words into common subword pieces. 'Unbelievable' becomes 'Un', 'believe', 'able'. Handles any input, unlimited vocabulary. Why tokenization matters: every token becomes an embedding the model learns. Bad tokenization means bad input representation.

items: Token — The smallest unit of text a model processes. Could be a word, subword, or character.
Word Tokenization — Splitting text into individual words based on spaces and punctuation boundaries.
Sentence Tokenization — Splitting text into individual sentences based on punctuation and capitalisation rules.

data.body: Machines cannot understand words the way humans do. They need numbers — every word must be converted into a numerical vector. Why text must be converted into numbers: neural networks only operate on numbers. Input must be a tensor of floating-point values. The most basic idea: assign each unique word a fixed numeric ID (one-hot encoding) or count how many times it appears (Bag of Words). Better representations capture meaning: words with similar meanings should have similar numerical vectors. This is the goal of modern NLP.

items: Text Representation — The process of converting human-readable text into numerical vectors that machine learning models can process.
Feature Representation — The numerical encoding of textual features — each dimension encodes some property of the text.

data.body: Bag of Words is the simplest text representation: count how many times each word from the vocabulary appears in a document. The vocabulary is the complete set of unique words across all documents. Each document becomes a vector with one entry per vocabulary word. Each entry in the vector stores the frequency of that word in the document. 'The cat sat' with vocabulary ['cat', 'sat', 'the'] becomes [1, 1, 1]. BoW is simple and interpretable but loses word order and context. 'Dog bites man' and 'Man bites dog' have identical representations. Despite its simplicity, BoW works well for topic classification and spam detection where word presence matters more than order.

items: Bag of Words — A text representation that counts word frequencies while ignoring word order and grammar.
Vocabulary — The complete set of unique tokens (words) across all documents in the dataset.
Document Vector — A numerical vector where each entry represents the frequency of a vocabulary word in the document.

data.text: Every NLP model, no matter how sophisticated, ultimately operates on numbers — not words. Text representation is the bridge between language and mathematics.

blocks.title: Text Processing Scans Language Like an Airport Scanner
blocks.subtitle: A scanner doesn't understand the bag — it breaks it into analysable signals. NLP doesn't understand text — it converts it into numbers that encode measurable properties.

panels.label: Real World
panels.description: An airport scanner converts a physical bag into an X-ray image — a numerical representation of densities. The scanner doesn't understand what a bag is; it understands numerical patterns that correlate with danger or safety.

panels.label: The Pattern
panels.description: Raw input gets converted to numbers. How you convert determines what patterns the computer can detect. A simple conversion counts words but loses their order. A better one preserves meaning.

panels.label: AI
panels.description: AI language models receive sequences of numbers, not words. Simple number schemes capture topic. More sophisticated ones capture meaning and context — who said what to whom.

blocks.insight: Choosing the right text representation is choosing what the model can see. Everything else in NLP flows from that decision.
blocks.reinforcement: Before any NLP model can learn, raw text must become numbers. Bag-of-words, TF-IDF, and tokenisation do this.

tokens = text.split()
print(f"Tokens: {tokens}")

blocks.solution:
text = "the cat sat on the mat"
tokens = text.split()
print(f"Tokens: {tokens}")
from collections import Counter
bow = Counter(tokens)
for word, count in bow.items():
    print(f"  '{word}': {count}")
blocks.hint: Tokenization splits text into individual tokens. Bag of Words counts how often each word appears.

data.body: Bag-of-words treats every word as isolated and unrelated. Word embeddings map words into a continuous vector space where similar words land near each other. The meaning of a word is encoded in its coordinates.
Each word is a dense vector of 100 to 1000 floating point numbers. Words with similar meanings have vectors that point in similar directions. The entire vocabulary lives in the same geometric space.

The cosine similarity between two word vectors measures semantic relatedness. Words like king and queen are close. King and car are far. This structure emerges automatically from training on large corpora — no one labels the meanings.

Train a small neural network to predict context words given a target word. The hidden layer weights become the word embeddings. The famous result: vector(King) minus vector(Man) plus vector(Woman) equals approximately vector(Queen).

Traditional embeddings give each word one fixed vector regardless of context. But bank means something different in river bank versus bank account. This limitation led to contextual embeddings in modern transformer models.

Embeddings trained on human text inherit human biases. Early word2vec embeddings associated doctor with men and nurse with women — simply because those associations appear in text. Debiasing is an active research area.

data.text: Word embeddings are coordinates in meaning space. Words that mean similar things end up near each other — automatically, without any human labelling.

blocks.title: Word Embeddings Map Meaning Like GPS Coordinates
blocks.subtitle: GPS coordinates encode physical location. Word embeddings encode semantic location. Close coordinates mean close places; close embeddings mean related meanings.

panels.label: Real World
panels.description: Paris and London are geographically close. Tokyo and Sydney are far. These spatial relationships are encoded in their GPS coordinates — nearby coordinates mean nearby cities. You can even compute: Paris minus France plus Germany equals approximately Berlin.

panels.label: The Pattern
panels.description: Coordinates encode relationships mathematically. Distance in the coordinate space means distance in the real space. Directions in the space encode relationships — north means increasing latitude.

panels.label: AI
panels.description: Word embeddings are semantic coordinates. King is close to Queen. Cat is close to Dog. And king minus man plus woman approximately equals queen. The directions in embedding space encode abstract relationships between concepts.

blocks.insight: Word embeddings turned semantics into geometry — and suddenly meaning could be measured, compared, and computed.
blocks.reinforcement: Semantically similar words cluster together in embedding space. Distance = dissimilarity. Direction = relationship.

blocks.title: Computing Word Similarity
blocks.instructions: Calculate similarity between word pairs using letter overlap (simplified embedding).
blocks.starterCode:
# Word similarity using character overlap
def similarity(word1, word2):
    common = len(set(word1) & set(word2))
    total = len(set(word1) | set(word2))
    return common / total if total > 0 else 0
pairs = [("king", "queen"), ("king", "apple"), ("apple", "orange")]
for w1, w2 in pairs:
    sim = similarity(w1, w2)
    print(f"{w1} ↔ {w2}: {sim:.2f}")
blocks.solution:
def similarity(word1, word2):
    common = len(set(word1) & set(word2))
    total = len(set(word1) | set(word2))
    return common / total if total > 0 else 0
pairs = [("king", "queen"), ("king", "apple"), ("apple", "orange")]
for w1, w2 in pairs:
    sim = similarity(w1, w2)
    print(f"{w1} ↔ {w2}: {sim:.2f}")
blocks.hint: Word embeddings place similar words close together in vector space. Similar words share more common letters.

data.body: A language model estimates the probability of a sequence of words. At its heart, every language model — from the simplest to GPT-4 — answers one question: given the words so far, what word is most likely to come next?

Predict the next word based on the previous N-1 words. A trigram model uses the previous 2 words. Simple but powerful: trained on enough text, trigrams can generate surprisingly coherent short sentences.

Perplexity measures how surprised a language model is by text it sees. Low perplexity means the model predicted well. A perplexity of 10 means the model was as confused as if choosing uniformly from 10 options at each step.

Replace n-gram counting with a neural network that reads the previous words as embeddings and predicts the next word distribution. Neural LMs generalise far better than n-grams because they learn continuous representations.

Temperature controls how random text generation is. Low temperature: always pick the most probable word — deterministic but repetitive. High temperature: more random — creative but potentially incoherent. Temperature 1.0 is the model's natural distribution.

data.text: Every large language model — GPT, Claude, Gemini — is at its core a next-token predictor trained on massive text. That simple objective produces remarkably general intelligence.

blocks.title: Language Models Navigate Text Like GPS Navigates Roads
blocks.subtitle: GPS uses a map of roads and probabilities — this road is likely given you are here. Language models use a map of word sequences and probabilities — this word is likely given you said this.

panels.label: Real World
panels.description: GPS doesn't pick the next road at random. Given your current location and direction, it estimates which road you are most likely on and will continue along. Context determines the most probable next state.

panels.label: The Pattern
panels.description: Current context determines what comes next. More context means better predictions. Past context is weighted by relevance. The model builds a probability map over all possible next steps and samples from it.

panels.label: AI
panels.description: Language models are trained to predict the next token given all previous tokens. After training on billions of sentences, they build a rich map of what words follow what contexts — and generate text by sampling from that map.

blocks.insight: Next-token prediction trained at scale produces models that appear to understand — because predicting text well requires modelling meaning.
blocks.reinforcement: Next-token prediction forces the model to learn grammar, facts, and reasoning — all from predicting the next word.

data.body: The Transformer architecture, introduced in 2017, is the foundation of every major language model today — GPT, BERT, Claude, Gemini. Its core innovation is the attention mechanism: letting every word in a sequence directly attend to every other word, regardless of distance.

Attention computes a weighted sum of value vectors, where the weights come from how much each query-key pair matches. Every word can directly look at every other word — and decide how much to pay attention to it.

Each token produces three vectors: a Query (what am I looking for?), a Key (what do I contain?), and a Value (what do I send if selected?). Attention weights are computed from Query-Key dot products — then applied to Values.

In self-attention, a sequence attends to itself. The word bank in river bank will attend strongly to river and weakly to money — producing a context-dependent representation that correctly captures the word's meaning in this specific sentence.

Run multiple attention operations in parallel, each focusing on different relationship types simultaneously. One head might track grammatical structure; another tracks coreference; another tracks semantic similarity. Concatenate all heads for a richer representation.

Each transformer block is: multi-head attention followed by a feed-forward network, with residual connections and layer normalisation around each. Stack 12 to 96 of these blocks and you have a large language model.

data.text: Attention solved the long-range dependency problem: any word can directly influence any other word, no matter how far apart they are in the sentence.

blocks.title: Attention Routes Understanding Like GPS Routes Traffic
blocks.subtitle: GPS doesn't give equal weight to every road — it focuses attention on the roads most relevant to your destination. Transformers do the same for words: focus on what matters, ignore what doesn't.

panels.label: Real World
panels.description: When navigating a city, you focus on roads that lead toward your destination. A road on the other side of the city gets zero attention — it is irrelevant. Attention is selective routing of information toward what matters.

panels.label: The Pattern
panels.description: Given a query (where am I going?), score every road (key) by its relevance, take a weighted average of the routes (values), and follow the highest-weight path. Apply this at every decision point simultaneously.

visual.conclusion: Meaning flows where it is needed

panels.label: AI
panels.description: The mechanism lets every word measure its relevance to every other word — even if they are far apart in the sentence. Words that are related get connected. Meaning flows directly across the entire sequence.

blocks.insight: Attention is the most important idea in modern AI. It made language modelling a solved problem at scale — and unlocked GPT, BERT, Claude, and every successor.
blocks.reinforcement: Attention scores which context tokens matter for each word. The Transformer learns WHAT to attend to — from data alone.

keyTakeaways.text: Tokenisation converts raw text into tokens — the atoms of NLP systems
Bag-of-words counts word frequencies but loses all word order
TF-IDF weights words by how distinctive they are to a specific document
Word embeddings place words in a continuous space where similar words are close
Word2Vec encodes semantic relationships as vector arithmetic
Language models predict the next token given all previous tokens
Attention lets every word directly attend to every other word in a sequence
The Transformer stacks multi-head attention and feed-forward blocks to process language
